module.title: Unit 6: Making a Difference: Future Forms - Will, Going to, Present Continuous
module.objective: Mampu menggunakan will (not), may (not), dan might (not) untuk prediksi; menggunakan first conditional dan unless dalam kalimat kondisional pertama; serta memahami kosakata lingkungan dan energi

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will explore texts about environmental challenges and future predictions. You will learn how to use future forms like will, may, and might, as well as the first conditional with unless to discuss protecting our natural world.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Future predictions using will, won't, may, and might, alongside first conditional sentences with if and unless.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Key environmental terms including endangered species, deforestation, pollution, and recycling.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific data and skimming paragraphs to identify main environmental themes.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of short texts about environmental conservation.
Locate specific details regarding endangered animals and climate change.
Recognize and apply future modals and first conditional structures correctly.

contextWarmup.prompt: What is one major problem affecting wildlife habitats around the world today?
options: Loss of natural forests due to human activity and agriculture
Too many trees growing in city parks and residential areas
An increase in clean energy projects in rural communities
contextWarmup.explanation: Human activities like deforestation and agriculture destroy natural habitats, making many animal species endangered.

rules: Use will and won't to make confident predictions about future events based on present facts.
Use may, may not, might, and might not to express uncertainty about future possibilities.
Use the first conditional with if plus present simple in the condition clause and will in the result clause.
Use unless to mean if not when stating an alternative condition.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Will with May and Might
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use will when they are not certain about a future event. Use may or might when you are guessing.
commonTrap.wrong: If we clean the beach, we will save all turtles for sure, but I am not certain.
commonTrap.correct: If we clean the beach, we might save many turtles, but we cannot be entirely certain.

content.passageTitle: Our Planet in Danger: What Does the Future Hold?
paragraphs: Our planet is facing serious environmental challenges today. In many parts of the world, widespread deforestation destroys the natural habitats of thousands of animals. Because of this, many species are now endangered, and some might even become extinct in the next few decades if we do not take action. Furthermore, plastic waste in our oceans and rivers causes severe pollution, harming marine animals and fragile ecosystems.

However, there is still hope for the future. If communities work together, we will see significant improvements. Many towns are starting to recycle more household waste and use renewable energy sources like solar power. Unless people change their daily habits, temperatures will continue to rise and polar ice caps will melt faster. Every single person can make a positive difference by taking small steps today.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Future Predictions and Conditional Actions

content.summary: Practical guide on writing future predictions, possibilities, and first conditional sentences about environmental issues in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Making Certain Predictions with Will
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + will / won't + base verb + time expression
blueprintItems.example: In ten years, cities will use more renewable energy.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Expressing Possibility with May and Might
blueprintItems.example: Temperatures may rise further if carbon emissions continue.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Building First Conditional Sentences
blueprintItems.formula: If + present simple, subject + will / won't + base verb
blueprintItems.example: If we protect local forests, wildlife will survive.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not put a comma before the main clause when the 'if' clause comes second.
mechanicsRules.badExample: We will save energy, if we turn off lights.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We will save energy if we turn off lights.
mechanicsRules.why: Commas are only needed after introductory subordinate clauses, not when the condition follows the main clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use present simple tense in the condition clause, not future tense.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If governments will act now, pollution will decrease.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If governments act now, pollution will decrease.
mechanicsRules.why: In first conditional sentences, the if-clause takes the present simple form while the main clause takes will.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first word of every sentence and major environmental nouns when used as proper titles.
mechanicsRules.badExample: unless we protect the amazon rainforest, nature will suffer.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Unless we protect the Amazon Rainforest, nature will suffer.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentence starts and proper geographical locations require standard English capitalization.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'will' to make a firm future prediction:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is certain that temperatures will increase next year.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'will increase' directly with the subject.
targetAnswers: Temperatures will increase next year.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To express future certainty, use 'will' followed by the base verb 'increase'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the grammatical error in the following first conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If we will plant more trees, air quality will improve.
practicumQuestions.hint: Remove the word 'will' from the if-clause.
targetAnswers: If we plant more trees, air quality will improve.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In first conditional sentences, the condition clause requires the present simple tense (plant), not future tense (will plant).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'unless' instead of 'if not':
practicumQuestions.promptText: If people do not stop wasting energy, bills will rise.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'If people do not' with 'Unless people'.
targetAnswers: Unless people stop wasting energy, bills will rise.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not', so it replaces negative conditional clauses directly.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence to show uncertainty using 'might':
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is possible that pandas will become extinct.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'might become' for weak possibility.
targetAnswers: Pandas might become extinct.
Panda bears might become extinct.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Might' expresses possibility in the present or future, replacing phrases like 'it is possible that'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this affirmative prediction into a negative prediction using 'won't':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Fossil fuels will last forever.
practicumQuestions.hint: Change 'will' to 'won't' or 'will not'.
targetAnswers: Fossil fuels won't last forever.
Fossil fuels will not last forever.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Won't' is the contracted negative form of 'will' used for future predictions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: if we protect the arctic, polar bears will survive.
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the first word and the proper noun Arctic.
targetAnswers: If we protect the Arctic, polar bears will survive.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Sentences must start with capital letters, and proper regions like the Arctic require capitalization.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the first conditional sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If governments (invest) in renewable energy, pollution will decrease.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the present simple form for 'governments'.
targetAnswers: If governments invest in renewable energy, pollution will decrease.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Plural subjects like 'governments' take the base form 'invest' in present simple conditional clauses.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the certainty to a possibility using 'may not':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Some animal species will definitely survive the climate crisis.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'will definitely' with 'may not' or adjust to uncertainty.
targetAnswers: Some animal species may not survive the climate crisis.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'May not' indicates a moderate possibility that something will fail to happen.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Put the first conditional clauses in the correct order without changing meaning when 'if' is placed second:
practicumQuestions.promptText: We will save water / if we fix leaking pipes
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'We will save water' followed by 'if we fix leaking pipes'.
targetAnswers: We will save water if we fix leaking pipes.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When the 'if' clause comes second, no comma is needed between the main clause and the conditional clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete first conditional sentence (at least 8 words) about reducing plastic waste:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Write a sentence starting with: 'If everyone uses reusable bags...'
practicumQuestions.hint: Complete the thought with a result using 'will'.
targetAnswers: If everyone uses reusable bags, plastic waste will decrease significantly.
If everyone uses reusable bags, ocean pollution will drop.
If everyone uses reusable bags, we will protect marine life.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A complete first conditional sentence pairs a present simple condition with a future 'will' result.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Making a Difference and Future Forms

content.summary: This module focuses on speaking clearly about environmental issues and future predictions using will, going to, and the present continuous. You will practice connecting words smoothly and using correct sentence stress to sound natural.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to weak forms in auxiliary verbs like will and going to. When speaking fast, 'going to' often sounds like 'gonna', but in formal B1 speaking tasks, you should articulate clearly.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.target: Stress content words and weaken grammar words
pillars.explanation: In sentences like 'We will protect the forest', the key words are 'protect' and 'forest'. Say them with more volume and pitch change.

pillars.name: Intonation in Predictions
pillars.target: Use rising and falling tones appropriately
pillars.explanation: Use a falling tone when stating firm predictions with will or going to, and a rising tone when introducing conditional clauses.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the primary stress remains on the second syllable for both words.
The stress stays on the second syllable when adding suffixes.
Notice how the stress shifts to the third syllable from the end when forming the noun.
Longer words ending in -tion always shift the primary stress to the syllable immediately preceding the suffix.
